profile.name: Abisola Morohunfolu
profile.biography: I build across the interface and the systems behind it. My work spans accessibility products, practical tools, and projects that help me understand how things work.

notes.title: From setup to results.
notes.text: Assessment setup and performance review belong to the same workflow. At TestAssessify, I helped lead frontend work across both.

notes.title: Following the code.
notes.text: In CodeCanvas, I’m exploring how much context a static graph can give a reviewer, and where it needs to admit uncertainty.

projects.title: Equally.ai
projects.summary: Bringing AI into accessibility workflows so teams can turn website issues into practical recommendations.
projects.contribution: AWS Bedrock integration, AI-assisted accessibility recommendations, and the customer experience around them.

children.text: Finding an accessibility issue is only the starting point. Teams also need to understand what to change. I integrated AWS Bedrock into the recommendation workflow to help bridge that gap.
I implemented support for text recommendations, image descriptions, and alt-text checks. The integration used the context of an issue to return suggestions the product could present for review.
Working with the engineering team, I connected these capabilities to the existing workflow. AI suggestions became part of the process of reviewing and addressing accessibility issues.
I also worked on customer interfaces, Flowy’s browser experience, and public audits. These tools helped teams find issues and use the platform’s recommendations while working on their websites.

Supporting work included copying website configurations, filtering and exporting integration records, and making billing and invoices accessible through the product. Each piece connected a customer task to the service behind it.

A customer’s renewal should be reflected in their website access. I helped build a process that compared payment-provider records with the product’s subscription records and corrected supported differences.
This work addressed cases where the product held an older expiration date after a renewal, helping keep payment information and customer access aligned.
Integrating AI meant thinking beyond the model response: what context it needed, how a suggestion appeared in the product, and how someone would use it to move forward.
Working across the interface and supporting services helped me approach features as complete customer workflows.

introduction: Equally.ai: bringing AI into accessibility work.

projects.title: Room Planner
projects.summary: See how a room fits before moving furniture. Compare layouts, edit dimensions, and take a plan with you.
projects.contribution: I built the planning experience, shared document model, device persistence, exports, and hosted snapshot workflow.

gallery.alt: Room Planner floor plan with measured furniture and room controls
gallery.caption: The same room document in the 2D editor.

gallery.alt: Read-only Room Planner shared snapshot on a mobile screen
gallery.caption: The shared viewer on a narrow screen.

children.text: The 2D editor and 3D view read the same room document. Dimensions, placement, openings, and finishes stay connected when switching views.
Separate renderers let each view do its job while the document owns the room. Fit notes report bounds, collisions, door swings, and nearby gaps; they do not certify a walking route.

sections.title: A useful plan on one device

children.text: Planning works with device storage and no account. Independent alternatives make it possible to compare arrangements without overwriting the original.
Exports include a dimensioned PDF, floor-plan image, furniture CSV, and a restorable plan file. Accounts and cloud synchronization are deferred.
Hosted links contain an immutable snapshot. Recipients can inspect it or save an independent copy. Editing the original room does not change an existing link.
Links expire after 30 days. The creating device keeps the management secret needed to revoke a link. Device planning continues when the sharing API is unavailable.

cover.alt: Room Planner showing a furnished living room in 3D beside finish controls
cover.caption: A real room in the planner, with editable wall and furniture finishes.

projects.statusNote: Device-first planning and snapshot sharing. Accounts and cloud synchronization are deferred.

projects.title: System Playground
projects.summary: Make runtime behavior visible. Follow requests through the event loop, queues, and worker pool.
projects.contribution: I built a simulation-first engine and an interactive Node.js board, with reusable simulation and UI packages.

children.text: The Node.js board shows request ingress, event loop phases, queues, the call stack, and libuv workers. It is a simulation designed to explain behavior, not a live profiler.
The engine is separated from simulations and the UI so new explorations can reuse the runtime. React render-cycle and concurrency explorations remain future extensions.

cover.alt: System Playground showing event loop phases, queues and worker activity
cover.caption: The Node.js simulation board. This is a model of runtime behavior.

projects.statusNote: The Node.js board is implemented. Additional runtime explorations are in progress.

projects.title: TestAssessify
projects.summary: Helping hiring teams set up assessments and track candidate performance in one place.
projects.contribution: Helped lead frontend development for assessment setup and the admin dashboard at my previous employer.

children.text: TestAssessify helps hiring teams assess candidates against the requirements of a role. The platform supports choosing assessments from a library or creating custom assessments.

The dashboard brought performance information into the team’s review workflow, helping administrators understand how candidates performed and use those results when deciding whom to progress.

projects.title: CodeCanvas
projects.summary: Explore a TypeScript codebase, follow static call relationships, and review how a branch changes the system.
projects.contribution: I built the local analyzer, architecture canvas, guided trace views, and review workflow.

sections.title: Read the structure, then follow a path

children.text: CodeCanvas loads a TypeScript project with ts-morph and resolves modules, symbols, routes, and calls into a browsable graph. Architecture, guided traces, branch review, and planning are separate ways to inspect that graph.
Trace views follow static code relationships. Edges can be exact, inferred, or ambiguous; untyped calls and runtime-dependent providers limit what the analyzer can resolve.
Branch review groups changed symbols with affected entry points and data writes. Focus and context views help narrow a large graph without pretending the analysis is complete.
The tool runs locally against a selected checkout. It is a code exploration aid rather than a substitute for tests or runtime observation.

projects.statusNote: A local development tool. Traces represent static analysis, not recorded runtime execution.
